At the beginning of the IELTS test, the examiner usually asks you simple questions and you can just give simple answers like this.
Can you please tell me your full name?
Maximus Decimus Meridius. And what should I call you?
Just Max is fine. Where are you from, Max?
Sparta. Can I see your identification, please?
Here you go. Thank you.

title: That'll teach you!
sourceTitle: That'll teach you!: The English We Speak
description: Feifei đi chơi khuya, sáng ngủ quên, đến muộn và luộm thuộm. "That'll teach you!" = đáng đời, lần sau chừa nhé!

segments.text: Hello, and welcome to The English We Speak with me, Neil and errr... where's Feifei?
Sorry I'm late. Hello!
Goodness, it's not like you to be late.
You're always so punctual and...
smartly dressed. But today you look a mess - If you don't mind me saying.
I do mind you saying, Neil.
It's been a very stressful morning.
I didn't have time to shower, iron my clothes or even have breakfast.
Hmm. Did you get up late by any chance?
Yes, you're right.
I forgot to set my alarm last night.
So I overslept!
Has this got anything to do with you going out last night?
I suppose you're going to tell me you had such a great time, you stayed out later than expected?
Yes, how did you guess?
I had one of the best nights out for a long time - but I'm regretting it now!
Ah well, that'll teach you for staying out late - enjoying yourself!
'That'll teach me'?
I'm not going to school - nobody is going to 'teach me' not to stay out late.
It's just a saying, Feifei.
You might say it to someone to suggest that they should learn the bad effects of doing something and not repeat it in the future.
In other words, your stress this morning is a suitable punishment for staying out late last night - you won't do it again.
You sound like my parents!
These examples might explain the phrase better...
You lent some money to Dan and he didn't pay you back - that'll teach you!
My brother got a speeding ticket for driving too fast down the High Street - that'll teach him!
The footballer got a red card for his bad tackle and now he'll miss playing in the final - that'll teach him!
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English and we're hearing about the phrase 'that'll teach you'
which is said to someone to mean they should learn from the bad effects of what they've done.
I guess we could also say 'it serves you right!'?
Yes, it's a very informal but blunt way of saying 'your suffering is your own fault'.
And for you it's true.
But do you know what, Neil - despite my suffering, I had a really good night out.
Oh did you?
And who did you have this 'great night out' with?
Everyone from the office.
We all went to the pub and then onto a nightclub.
That'll teach you for leaving the office early, Neil.
You left too early and you missed out!
Hmm. That's enough teaching for one day. I'm off. Bye!

title: A walk in the park
sourceTitle: A walk in the park: The English We Speak
description: Neil tự tin chạy 5 km "dễ như đi dạo trong công viên"… rồi về đích thở không ra hơi. "A walk in the park" = rất dễ.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Feifei.
And I'm Neil.
Hey thanks for joining me today, Feifei.
No problem, Neil.
I wanted to give you my support for your first run in the park.
Well, this run in the park is only five kilometres.
I know, but you're not particularly fit and you haven't done much training.
Oh don't worry about that - this will be a walk in the park!
Err Neil - I hope you're not thinking of walking around the park - this is a run, a run in the park!
I have no intention of walking - it's just an expression that means it's easy to do, especially compared to other activities.
I'm glad to hear that because it's just about to start - let's hope you really do find it easy!
Don't worry, I will have finished by the time you hear these examples...
I've been studying for so long, this exam should be a walk in the park.
Oh don't worry about me, I've trekked in the Himalayas, this hill will be a walk in the park!
The job at the bank will be a walk in the park - you studied economics at university!
You're listening to The English We Speak from BBC Learning English - and Neil has been using the phrase 'a walk in the park' to explain that a run in the park is easy,
especially when compared to other activities - like running a full marathon, for example.
But where is Neil now?
...here I am.
Oh, that was hard.
So that run wasn't a walk in the park then?
That's a shame.
Why's that?
Well, I thought that if running in the park was too easy, you could train for next year's London Marathon.
It's over 42 kilometres - that would be no walk in the park.
Err, could we just park that idea, please?!
I'm going to do another activity to keep fit and healthy.
Oh yes, what's that?
Walking. In the park!
Good idea. Bye! Bye.

title: Left on read
sourceTitle: Left on read: The English We Speak
description: Roy đọc tin nhắn mà không trả lời vì… đang ăn chuối. Đến khi biết tin nhắn mời đi xem nhạc miễn phí thì đã muộn!

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak with me, Feifei… ..and me, Roy.
In this programme, we have an expression which describes when someone has read the message you’ve sent them, but hasn’t replied.
That reminds me, Roy - did you get my message yesterday?
Oh… yes, I did.
I read it and then totally forgot to answer you.
Was it something important?
I can’t believe it!
You completely ignored my message.
I got left on read!
What’s the colour ‘red’ got to do with the fact I forgot to reply?
Red is actually my favourite colour.
Not red the colour, but ‘read’ as in the past of ‘read’.
Ahhh, got you.
Sorry, I didn’t mean to leave you on read.
It’s just I was in the middle of something … and then I got distracted ….and then… OK.
Roy. I understand!
What was so important that you couldn’t reply?
I was eating a really nice banana, and then I just forgot… sorry.
That’s a terrible excuse – it’s a good thing we’re friends or I might think you were ignoring me.
Anyway, let’s listen to these examples…
I can’t believe I was left on read.
I sent him a message and I can see he’s looked at it, but he hasn’t replied!
My partner always leaves me on read.
They get really distracted and then don't message me back.
You shouldn’t assume the worst if you get left on read.
If someone reads your message and doesn’t reply, they might be really busy and planning to respond later.
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English and we’re talking about the expression ‘left on read’.
We use this when someone has read a message, but hasn’t replied.
So, were you really eating a banana and that’s why you left me on read?
Yeah, sorry. Well, I was also playing video games which might have been the main reason.
Haha – I knew it!
Well the next time I want to offer you free tickets to the ‘Rob’s Rolling Biscuit’ rock concert,
hopefully you’ll reply and not just leave me on read!
What!?! Free tickets?!
Let me read the message again!
Can I still have the tickets?
Sorry, it’s too late now.
I gave them to Neil.
He didn’t leave me on read.
Bye, Roy. Bye.

title: The best of both worlds
sourceTitle: The best of both worlds: The English We Speak
description: Rob khoe được cả nhịp sống thành phố lẫn bình yên ở quê — cho đến khi tàu về làng bị huỷ. "The best of both worlds" = vẹn cả đôi đường.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak, with you Rob...
...and you, Feifei.
Hey Rob, how are you enjoying your new life in the countryside?
It's great Feifei.
When I get home at night, I get to smell the fresh air and look out on green fields.
Yes, the country life is for me.
But come on Rob, you must miss the bright lights and the excitement of living in the city?
Well, I get that by coming to work right here in the centre of London.
I have a great night out and then slip off to the peace and quiet of the country. Perfect!
Perfect? I don't think so - the countryside is too quiet.
The city is the only place for me.
No way. I've got the best of both worlds - excitement in the city, relaxation in the country.
The best of both worlds - you think you get the advantages of two very different things at the same time.
Yes that's right.
Let's hear some examples of the phrase 'the best of both worlds' in action...
Working part-time means I get the best of both worlds: time with the kids and a steady income.
Our hotel is by the beach and just a short train ride away from the city, so we get the best of both worlds.
We get the best of both worlds with our new car: excellent fuel efficiency and great acceleration and speed.
So the phrase 'the best of both worlds' means you have the benefits of two different things and none of the disadvantages.
But surely Rob there must be some negative things about living in the country?
Such as?
No shops, no pubs or clubs, having a long commute to work every day.
I can cope - anyway, commuting by train is fine - time to relax and shake off the stress of the city.
Maybe not today Rob.
Why? My news feed says there's been a major signal failure - all trains to your village are cancelled!
Cancelled? Grrr. So I can't get home!
Err, any chance I could sleep on your sofa tonight?
Ha, so maybe it's not always possible to have the best of BOTH worlds Rob?
Maybe! Bye. Bye.

title: A wake-up call
sourceTitle: A wake-up call: The English We Speak
description: Rob đi muộn, thở hổn hển vì chạy ra ga. Feifei bảo đây là "a wake-up call" — không phải chuông báo thức đâu, mà là lời cảnh tỉnh!

segments.text: Hello everyone. This is The English We Speak with me, Feifei… and… oh no, Rob is late again!
Sorry I’m late, I missed my train and I had to wait for the next one… Are you OK, Rob?
You’re very breathless.
Well, you would be if you had run to the station and from the station to the office.
Hmmm, it’s not that far, Rob!
I think this is a wake-up call.
A wake-up call?
No, I set my alarm – I got out of bed – it just seems to take longer to walk to the station these days.
I didn’t mean your alarm, Rob.
‘A wake-up call’ is a warning that you need to change your current situation before it gets any worse.
And what is my ‘current situation’?
You’re unfit – you need to do some more exercise!
Let’s hear some examples of ‘a wake-up call’ shall we?
Martha’s bad test results were a wake-up call for her to work harder before her final exams.
The store’s poor sales results are a wake-up call for the business to move with times and sell more fashionable clothes.
The recent extreme weather is a wake-up call for us all to do something about climate change.
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English, and in this programme we’re learning about the phrase ‘a wake-up call’,
which means a warning to change your current situation and stop things from getting any worse.
It’s time to change - like Rob’s fitness!
So Rob, how are you going to change your current situation?
Well, that’s easy – I’m going to get a later train.
More time in bed!
I wouldn’t, Rob – otherwise you’ll get another ‘wake-up call’.
Who from? The boss – he hates people being late all the time.
So if you’re not punctual, you might get the sack!
Oh right, I’m off!
Where are you going?
To do some exercise.
Like you said, I need to get fit – quickly!
Bye. Good luck, Rob.

title: Catch-22
sourceTitle: Catch-22: The English We Speak
description: Feifei trượt phỏng vấn vì thiếu kinh nghiệm — nhưng không có việc thì sao có kinh nghiệm? "Catch-22" = tình huống không lối thoát.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak.
It's Feifei here…
…and hello, it's Rob here too.
Oh Feifei, why the glum face?
I didn't get it.
Get it?
I didn't get the job.
Oh yes yes, the job – you went for a new job – one you really really wanted.
One that you said would be perfect for you.
Clearly I am not.
Look at this rejection letter, it says I did not have enough experience.
How dare they!
But if I don't do the job, how do I get the experience?
Oh dear, it sounds like catch-22.
Catch-22? Is that some kind of qualification I need?
Nope, it just describes a situation where you can't win.
Basically, you can't do one thing until you have done another thing which you can't do until you have done the first thing.
So it's an impossible situation.
It is. Let's hear some examples of this phrase in action…
I need my parents' car, but my mum says I need permission from my dad,
then my dad says I need permission from my mum.
I can't get permission from either.
So I'm in a catch-22 situation.
To apply for a short-term student visa to study English in the UK,
you have to be able to speak some English but you want to come to England to learn English!
It's catch-22 for many potential students.
You're listening to The English We Speak and Rob has told me I'm in a catch-22 situation.
That's a situation I cannot win.
Yes Feifei, so you can't get a new job without some experience of doing it
but you can't get the experience without doing the job.
So it's catch-22!
It's a strange phrase Rob.
Yes, it comes from the title of a book, Catch-22,
written by Joseph Heller in 1961 which describes bureaucratic constraints on soldiers in World War II.
But look Feifei, don't be too sad about the job, you've got plenty of experience for doing this job.
That's because I've been here for 40 years!
But we respect you for expertise, especially in one task.
What's that?
Making the tea.
Now could you put the kettle on please?
Oh, I really need a new job.
Bye. Bye.

title: Not gonna lie
sourceTitle: Not Gonna Lie: The English We Speak
description: "Not gonna lie, you look tired" — tiếng lóng để nói thật lòng (hoặc tự khen). Neil và Feifei tranh nhau làm "best presenter".

segments.text: Welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Neil.
And I'm Feifei.
You're a pretty polite person, aren't you, Feifei?
Well, thanks. I don't know.
I do try to be!
That was a very polite answer!
But sometimes we want to say things that are very honest, or that others might not want to hear.
For example, I ask you: "Do I look tired today?"
Well, I could directly say: "Yes, you do look a bit tired."
Or you could start with today's slang expression 'not gonna lie'.
Not gonna lie Feifei, you do look a little tired.
I know, I need to get to bed earlier!
'Gonna' of course, is short for 'going to'.
Using this phrase indicates that you're choosing to be honest rather than polite.
It's not only used for honest criticism, we might also use it before something we're very proud of, or something we boast about.
For example: I love recording these programmes.
Though I'm not gonna lie, I'm the best presenter in this team.
Whoah, that's enough.
I'm sure everyone listening agrees that I'm the best presenter.
Of course you're a fantastic presenter, Feifei.
Just an example!
Talking of examples, let's hear a few more.
Fancy coming round for dinner tomorrow?
Absolutely. If you're making your famous roast?
Oh yes. Not gonna lie, it's the best roast in town!
Slow down! You really are a terrible driver Mark, not gonna lie.
Not gonna lie, I absolutely love my job.
I feel so happy when I walk through the office door every day.
That last example sounds just like me.
Especially as I'm the best presenter.
OK, OK, that joke is getting old now.
You're right. OK, one more thing.
This phrase 'not gonna lie'...
Yes? Not gonna lie, I think some people use it too much!
Yes, it's become a popular phrase on social media.
Usually accompanied by a photo of someone on holiday at the beach with a post saying "Not gonna lie, it's stunning here!"
The kind of post that makes me feel jealous when I'm stuck in the office.
But I thought you loved your job?!
Oh, I do.
And yes, you are a very good presenter, Neil.
That makes me feel much better, not gonna lie. Bye.

title: Barking up the wrong tree
sourceTitle: Barking up the wrong tree: The English We Speak
description: Feifei nghi Rob mách sếp chuyện cô làm đổ cà phê. Rob: "You're barking up the wrong tree!" = nghi nhầm người rồi.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Feifei...
And I'm Rob.
Hello. Errr, Feifei, you're looking a bit angry.
Me, angry! I am angry.
Oh no, what's the problem?
I think you know Rob.
Somebody told the boss that I spilt coffee over his computer yesterday - and now he's angry with me.
Oh no. What kind of mean and horrible person would try and get you into trouble?
You and the boss were the only people left in the office last night. Hmmm?
Whoa - hold on Feifei.
If you are implying it was me who told the boss, then you are barking up the wrong tree.
Please don't make me any angrier by saying that I am like a dog!
No, no Feifei.
Just calm down.
I should be angry because you are making the wrong assumption about who told the boss, OK?
That's what I mean by barking up the wrong tree - you want to blame someone but you got the wrong person.
I didn't even know you had done it.
OK, I'm sorry.
So the phrase 'barking up the wrong tree' means making the wrong assumption when trying to achieve something.
Shall we hear some examples while I make you a coffee to say sorry...?
If you think I have enough spare cash to pay for your holiday, then you're barking up the wrong tree.
You're barking up the wrong tree if you think I was the one who said you were leaving.
It wasn't me!
You're barking up the wrong tree if you think I'm going to lend you my car.
I've seen how you drive!
You're listening to The English We Speak.
We're talking about the phrase 'barking up the wrong tree'.
It means to make a wrong assumption about someone or something.
The phrase can also mean doing something in a way that will not work - you're basically wasting your time.
Like a detective trying to solve a crime by obviously arresting the wrong man - he's barking up the wrong tree.
Ok Rob understood - and here's your coffee to say sorry for barking up the wrong tree.
Thanks - make sure you don't spill it this time.
The boss would be really angry!
...what did I say?
If I find out you did tell the boss, I'll make sure to bark up the right tree, OK?
Oh Feifei, I hope your bark is worse than your bite. Bye. Bye

title: Up your game
sourceTitle: Up your game: The English We Speak
description: Neil nhờ Feifei viết tin nhắn mời bạn gái đi cà phê: "you need to up your emoji game!" = phải nâng trình lên. Kết thúc bất ngờ!

segments.text: Welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Neil.
And I'm Feifei.
Actually, Feifei, can you help me with something?
Go on.
There's this girl I like.
I want to ask her for coffee.
But I don't want to seem too serious or creepy or anything. Just friendly.
And you're writing her a message? OK.
I just can't find the words.
Easy. Stick a couple of emojis on there.
Much less formal!
You mean, like, a smiley face?
Yeah, but those are so last year.
Maybe a love heart?
Seriously? That's a bit too much.
You need to up your emoji game!
My emoji game...
like an emoji of a video game...
or a football?
No. The phrase 'to raise your game', or 'to up your game', means to improve.
Yes, it's a good phrase.
Feifei, you're not working hard enough, you need to up your game!
That's not true...
but good use of up your game.
The phrase has now developed a bit.
We often add what we're trying to improve before the word 'game'.
Like this:
I never finish novels.
I need to up my reading game.
I badly need to work on my interview game before my big interview next week.
You could do with a bit more exercise, mate.
You should raise your running game!
Great. Hope those examples help.
Any progress with that text message?
Here goes: "Lucy.
Please have a coffee with me tomorrow.
And then some coffee emojis.
Well, it's direct!
But I still think we need to up your emoji game.
Actually, and your texting game.
Oh, and your dating game...
We've got a lot of work to do!
Oh, ok. Well I already sent the message.
Let's hope it works!
And she's replied already.
No way, what did she say?
Neil. I thought you'd never ask!
I'd love to have coffee.
3pm?" And then a couple of big smiley emojis.
Wow, congratulations. Maybe it's me who needs to up my game.
Looks like it! Bye.

title: Don't rub it in!
sourceTitle: Rub it in: The English We Speak
description: Feifei bảo Neil "don't rub it in" (đừng nhắc mãi nữa) — và Neil… không thoa kem chống nắng. Về như con tôm luộc!

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak.
I'm Neil and joining me in this programme is Feifei.
Hi. Beautiful day today, isn't it?
Blazing sunshine. It's so warm.
Yes it is, and luckily for you, your shift is finished after this programme, isn't it?
Yep! But you have to stay here till evening on the late shift.
Ahhh I'm off to the park to enjoy the sun.
I'd better buy some sun cream, eh?
Don't rub it in!
OK. See you later.
Two hours later.
My word, Neil!
What's happened to you?
You look like a lobster!
It's very hot and sunny out there.
But what about the sun cream?
You told me 'not to rub it in' Feifei!
OK, I think I need to explain something.
We use the expression 'to rub something in' when a person keeps mentioning something another person wants to forget.
When I said 'don't rub it in' I was fed up of hearing about your wonderful afternoon in the sun while I'm stuck here in the office!
Ah. So I actually should have rubbed in this sun cream.
Let's hear some examples...
Don't rub it in.
I know you beat me at tennis but you don't have to keep mentioning the score.
Carlos got into Oxford but I didn't.
That's bad enough, but he keeps rubbing it in by talking about it all the time.
This is The English We Speak and in this programme we're learning the phrase to 'rub it in'.
If a person 'rubs it in' it means they keep mentioning something another person wants to forget.
I want to forget that I've got such a terrible sunburn.
Well I won't rub it in and talk about that sun cream you should have...
should have rubbed in.
Thanks Feifei. Ouch!
Bye! Bye!

title: Why are you having a go at me?
sourceTitle: Have a go: The English We Speak
description: Áo chưa là, dính sốt cà chua, chưa cạo râu… Feifei "has a go at" Neil (chê trách). "Have a go" còn có nghĩa là "thử làm".

segments.text: Morning Neil. In a rush today, were you?
Just a bit, Feifei.
You know, kids, breakfast, commute.
The usual. Why?
Well - I noticed your shirt isn't ironed.
Very attentive of you.
And your shirt has ...
ketchup on it?
Oops, yes - beans for breakfast.
And you haven't shaved, have you?
Well, no. Erm...
You really do need to make more of an effort.
Feifei, why are you having a go at me?
Relax, Neil. I'm just giving you the opportunity to use the phrase we are teaching, which is: 'have a go'!
Well that's a relief.
'To have a go at someone', as we've just seen, means to criticise someone.
That's right. Here are some examples.
The boss really had a go at Michaela after she offended our clients.
Susie had a go at her husband last night.
He'd forgotten all about her birthday.
Why do you always have a go at me?
Why can't you say something nice?
That's our phrase.
'To have a go at someone' - which means to criticise someone.
There. Can we be nice to each other now?
Well, we can have a go!
Ah, very clever.
'To have a go' has another meaning - 'to try'.
Yes - if you have a go at something, you try it.
Why don't you have a go at making an example sentence, Feifei?
Ok then. I'm going to have a go at cooking a Thai curry from scratch.
Tasty. 'To have a go' meaning 'to try'.
And one last thing, Feifei.
Do I really look scruffy?
Not at all.
Though you could shave once in a while.
I'll have a go.
Just for you Feifei. Feifei Bye.

title: A taste of your own medicine
sourceTitle: A taste of your own medicine: The English We Speak
description: Feifei bị cảm và uống thuốc vị "dâu" kinh khủng. "A taste of your own medicine" = gậy ông đập lưng ông — và ai mới là người hay sai bảo?

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Feifei…
and I'm Neil.
Hey Feifei, it sounds like you might have a cold?
I think I have – sore throat, blocked nose.
I feel terrible.
That's why I'm taking this medicine.
That's probably a good idea.
Medicine is usually good for making you feel better but how does it taste?
Well, it's supposed to taste of strawberries but to be honest it's just horrible!
That's why I never take the stuff – it's disgusting.
Have you heard the phrase 'a taste of your own medicine'?
No. Does it mean doing something horrible or unpleasant?
Sort of. It describes someone receiving the same, treatment or unpleasant experience that they have given to somebody else.
You know, like you're always bossing people around and then someone starts to boss you around?
I don't know what you mean Neil!
Anyway, it's quite a negative phrase.
It is. Let's hear some examples…
Our boss is so rude to us but finally somebody has answered back and now he's got a taste of his own medicine.
When I meet up with my boyfriend, he's always late
so this time I'm going to give him a taste of his own medicine and turn up late as well.
Deepak is always rude to the teacher but he was really offended when she gave him a taste of his own medicine and was rude back to him!
So that's 'a taste of your own medicine' which describes someone receiving the same treatment that they have given to somebody else. Excuse me!
Oh dear. It sounds like you need to take some more medicine.
If you mean literally taking the medicine, then yes.
But if you mean receiving the same treatment I've given to someone else, then no.
I can't believe you think I am always bossing people around.
I was just giving an example of the phrase.
I would never say you were bossy.
Good. Now why don't you go and make me a nice cup of tea?
Oh, OK, sure. See you.
And don't forget to close the door!
Yes. Sorry. I'll do that right now.
OK. See you later.
Ah, I feel better already. Bye.

title: Out of the loop
sourceTitle: Out of the loop: The English We Speak
description: Neil bỏ lỡ cuộc họp về chính sách "làm việc lành mạnh": không được ngồi, không cà phê… "Out of the loop" = không nắm thông tin.

segments.text: Hello, and welcome to The English We Speak.
I'm Feifei and with me is Neil.
Hi there.
Neil, what are you doing sitting down?
Presenting this programme – like we always do – sitting in a chair.
You clearly don't know about our new healthy working policy – no more sitting down – standing up is better for you!
Oh, alright then, I'll stand up if I have to.
Oh, Neil! No drinking coffee in the studio.
Health and safety!
Obviously, you missed our meeting about the new healthy working policy.
You are clearly out of the loop.
What? There's a loop I have to stand in now?
No, Neil. You missed our meeting where we discussed the new healthy working policy, and now you're out of the loop.

title: Present perfect or past simple? — 4 differences
sourceTitle: 'I've done' or 'I did'? - Ask BBC Learning English
description: 4 điểm khác nhau giữa hiện tại hoàn thành và quá khứ đơn: kết quả ở hiện tại, mốc thời gian đã kết thúc/chưa kết thúc, việc vẫn còn đúng đến nay, và trải nghiệm.

segments.text: Present perfect or past simple?
Maryam wants to find out about the differences.
This can be confusing as we use both for past events.
However, the present perfect has more of a link with the present.
Let's look at four main differences to help.
So, we can use both for things that happened in the past.
But if there's a result in the present, we tend to use the present perfect.
Oh, I've lost my phone.
Can you call me? So, I lost my phone in the past, but it is still lost now in the present.
I've lost my glasses. Can you see them anywhere?
However, if there isn't a result in the present, then we generally use the past simple.
The event is firmly in the past.
It doesn't affect our present.
I lost my phone last week, but someone handed it in.
Did you also hear there was a time phrase - 'last week'?
That brings me onto our next difference.
With finished time words like these, we use the past simple.
I bought myself some flowers yesterday.
With unfinished time words, we normally use the present perfect.
Here are some examples. I've bought so many clothes this year.
Careful though, sometimes these time words can be used with the past simple as well.
It depends on how the speaker views this time.
I haven't had coffee today.
I didn't have a coffee today.
So if I say 'I haven't had a coffee today', maybe it's midday.
The day is still happening.
I haven't had coffee today.
Can you make me a coffee, please?
At the end of the day, I might say 'I didn't have a coffee today'.
I used 'today', but I'm thinking of the day as finished.
Off to bed. Next, if the action started in the past but is still true or still happens now, we can use the present perfect.
I've lived in Brighton for eight years, so I moved here eight years ago, but I still live here now.
However, if the action started in the past and finished in the past, I use the past simple.
I lived in New Zealand for four years, so I lived in New Zealand in the past.
But I don't live there now - I live here.
Another example. They've been married for five years.
They got married five years ago, and they are still married today.
It's their anniversary on Sunday.
In this example, they were married for five years.
They are not married now, but they got divorced last year.
Finally, if you want to talk about an experience in your life and we're not saying when,
you can use the present perfect because your life is still happening.
I've seen the Northern Lights.
However, if you want to talk about a specific event in the past, then we use the past simple.
When I visited Iceland, I saw the Northern lights.
So even though I don't say when, we know that it was a time in the past.

title: Present perfect simple or continuous?
sourceTitle: Present perfect simple or continuous? - Ask BBC Learning English
description: "I've chopped the onions" hay "I've been chopping onions"? Năm điểm khác nhau: hoàn thành vs đang tiếp diễn, kết quả vs quá trình, bao nhiêu vs bao lâu, động từ chỉ trạng thái.

segments.text: 'I've done' or 'I've been doing'.
What's the difference? Let's look at this question from Juan.
I want to know: What is the difference between present perfect and present perfect continuous?
Sometimes they can be very similar.
I've worked at the BBC for 8 years.
I've been working at the BBC for 8 years.
So, here, both sentences are correct and they connect the past with the present.
But let's look at five differences.
Using the present perfect simple emphasises that an action is complete.
It has an effect on the present, but the action has finished.
Someone has eaten my chocolates!
They're all gone. Using the present perfect continuous emphasises that the action is ongoing.
Someone has been eating my chocolates.
There's only a few left.
The action may continue in the future.
We use the present perfect simple to focus on the result of an action.
I've chopped the onions. What's next?
So, the result is: the onions are ready.
We use the present perfect continuous to focus on the doing of an action.
I'm not crying - I've just been chopping onions.
So here, the focus is on doing the action itself – the chopping of onions, so doing this action made me cry.
We also use the present perfect continuous when we can see some evidence of an action that happened a short time ago.
The action is completed, but we can still see the evidence.
I've been cooking all day so the kitchen's a mess.
We use the present perfect simple to focus on how many, or how often.
It's rained every day this week.
I've had four coffees today.
We use the present perfect continuous if the focus is on how long – often with phrases like all morning, all day, for ages.
It's been raining all day!
I've been drinking coffee all morning, and I'm still tired!
Careful though: state verbs, we don't normally use in the continuous.
I've been knowing Beth for three years.
I've known Beth for three years.
And finally, we can use the present perfect continuous to emphasise that our situation is temporary.
I've broken my leg, so I've been working from home lately.

title: Past simple or past perfect?
sourceTitle: The past simple and past perfect tenses - English Learners' Questions
description: Dan giải đáp: "When was the last time you ate here?" — khi nào dùng quá khứ đơn, khi nào dùng quá khứ hoàn thành ("the film had already started").

segments.text: OK! This week's learner question comes from Niki from Hungary, who writes: The following sentence has been giving me a headache for weeks now.
Could you please give me the correct answer and justify it?
When was the last time you had eaten ate in this restaurant?
Two weeks ago. Ok, Niki, are you ready?
Here we go. So, in your example it has to be the past simple.
When was the last time you ate in this restaurant?
Two weeks ago. Now the past simple refers to finished periods of time or moments of time.
It refers to a definite past.
So, it’s often used with time adverbials such as: last night, some time ago, in 1985, earlier today,
at six o clock this morning, the last time, the first time, etc etc etc.
And don’t forget that the auxiliary verb is did.
For example: The first time I ever rode a horse was on my 7th birthday.
And the last time was 6 months ago.
The past simple can also be used to refer to repeated past events and past habits and past states.
For example: When I was small, we lived in a cottage by the sea and I played every day on the beach.
Now, the past perfect is formed using had a past participle verb.
And, we use it when we are already discussing the past and wish to refer back to an event that happened before this point.
For example: When I got to the cinema, the film had already started.
Now, the past perfect can also be used with words like after, as soon as, when and once,
but usually only to emphasise that one action is quite separate and independent and has finished before another one.
Remember, everything’s in the past.
So, compare these sentences: When I got out of the car, I bought a parking ticket.
These two are connected. One follows the other.
However, when I had got out of the car, a dog ran over to me.
These two events are unconnected and separate.

title: Future plans: present continuous, going to or will?
sourceTitle: Future tenses: present continuous, 'be going to', 'will' - English Learners' Questions
description: Câu chuyện ở sân bay: "I'm flying to Spain" (đã có vé), "I'm going to fly to Australia" (kế hoạch), "I will fly to Russia" (quyết định tức thời).

segments.text: This week's learner question comes from Christina from Austria, who asks:
Would you be able to explain the difference between "will" and "going to" when talking about the future, please?
Of course, Christina, it’s quite a common question.
I hope this answer helps.
So, there’s a difference between future predictions and future plans and we’re only going to be looking at future plans for the moment.
Please remember that these rules are a rough guide and sometimes native speakers bend or even break them – so be careful.
So, a man goes to the airport.
He’s carrying a suitcase. In the suitcase is a passport, some clothes, some sunglasses and a ticket.
He goes up to the check-in desk and he says to the lady there, “I’m flying to Spain later today.”
Notice this is the present continuous.
That’s for a future arrangement.
It’s called an arrangement because it’s like a plan, but he has the ticket, and the ticket is evidence of the plan.
This means that if the man were to disappear, the airline would still expect him to arrive for the flight.
That’s what the evidence means.
However, the lady behind the check-in desk says “Sorry.
No, that flight’s been cancelled.
But you can fly to Australia or to Russia.”
Well, this is a big decision, so the man goes to the cafe to think about it.
When he comes back he says, “Ok, I’m going to fly to Australia.”
That’s be going to for a future plan.
He’s had time to think about it in the cafe before speaking, but he doesn’t have a ticket so it’s not an arrangement.
But the lady behind the check-in desk says “Sorry!
You took too long in the cafe.
That flight has gone. But you can still fly to Russia.”
So, the man says, “Ok.
I will fly to Russia.”
That’s will for a future based on a decision made at the moment of speaking.”
He makes the decision at that time.
No plan existed before that.
Did you get it? That’s present continuous for a future arrangement.
It’s be going to for a future plan and it’s will for an instant decision made at that moment.

title: How to choose the correct tense — it's all about aspect
sourceTitle: How to choose the correct tense in English - BBC English Masterclass
description: Mọi thì trong tiếng Anh = thời gian + "aspect" (simple, continuous, perfect). Hiểu "tính cách" của từng aspect để chọn đúng thì.

segments.text: Are you tense about tense?
Well, don't be! In this session's masterclass I'll let you into a little secret of all English tenses - it's all about character. After this.
Ok guys. In this masterclass we're going to get a little bit theoretical, ok?
So try and hold on.
Tenses in English are made up of two things.
A time and an aspect.
Now almost all languages and cultures recognise three times: past, present and future.
But what about an aspect?
An aspect is the character of a verb.
It adds extra information to the verb's meaning and reflects the perception of the speaker.
Now, depending on who you talk to, there are between two and four aspects, but I like to say three.
They are simple, continuous and perfect and all three of them can be used in past, present and future.
The simple aspect is actually not an aspect at all.
It does not modify the verb in terms of its meaning, only in terms of its form.
And this is because, in all cases, the unmodified verb is enough to express exactly the meaning that the speaker wants to say at the time of speaking.
They broadly fall into three categories.
We have the long term general truth.
For example, I like studying English.
We have the instantaneous. For example, I now pronounce you man and wife.
And we have the habitual.
For example, I woke up every day at 6am last year.
The continuous aspect is formed with some sort of be plus verbING.
The focus of this aspect is primarily upon the duration of an event.
All progressive forms contain characteristics of temporariness, unfinishedness or in progress-ness.
The progressive aspect tends to disregard the end of an action and view the event from the centre.
So, an action might be happening at the moment of speaking.
For example, I'm making a video right now.
Or, around a certain time.
For example, before we met I was living in Scotland.
Or, simultaneously when another action occurs.
For example, When you get home, I'll be working in the office
The perfect aspect is formed with some version of have plus the past participle.
Perfect aspects focus on bridging two times together, and connecting events between one time and another, often through relevancy.
An event in the past might be relevant to the present moment.
An event in the future could be connected in some way to the present or the past.
Perfect verb phrases can describe states.
For example, I've loved you since I first met you.
Actions. For example, I will have gone to the gym by the time you get home.
And habits. For example, my father had started work at 9 o'clock every day for the last 20 years.
And of course we can link aspects to create perfect continuous verb phrases.
These combine the forms of their two base aspects.
For example, have plus been plus verbING, and they combine their meanings.
So we can create verb phrases which focus on actions or events with duration with relevancy to more than one time period.

title: The zero conditional — facts, habits & rules
sourceTitle: The zero conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + hiện tại đơn, hiện tại đơn: sự thật khoa học, thói quen cá nhân ("If I don't sleep well, I'm grumpy") và quy định ("If you don't buy a ticket, you get a fine").

segments.text: Hello, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English, and in this video you'll learn how to talk about facts using something called the zero conditional. Let's get started.
Now, we're often taught the zero conditional in the context of scientific facts.
Typical examples are: If you heat water, it boils.
If you mix red and blue paint, you get purple.
And that's true! But how often do you say things like that?
So the best thing for you to do is to hear real people using the zero conditional.
I asked my colleagues: what happens if you don't get a good night's sleep?
If I don't get a good night's sleep, I usually feel quite groggy, grumpy, and I generally can't concentrate very well.
If I don't get a good night's sleep, I can be a little bit spacey, so I don't really pay attention very well.
I find it really hard to know what's going on.
I have to drink lots of coffee, which probably makes it a lot worse.
If I don't get a good night's sleep, I'm not very happy.
Unfortunately, this does happen quite a lot.
So these are still facts.
They're truths about your personal experience, in a general sense, so notice the use of 'usually', 'generally' and 'this happens quite a lot'.
So, for example, Neil is usually quite happy, but if and when he doesn't sleep well - the condition - he isn't very happy.
And this happens quite a lot: it's a general truth.
Let's hear another example. Usually when I finish work, I play guitar.
So if I don't do that, then I kind of feel a bit stressed out maybe.
Here we have two general truths: So in general, when George finishes work, he plays guitar.
And again, in general, if he doesn't play guitar, he feels stressed out.
In a similar way, we can also use the zero conditional to talk about rules and laws.
If you travel on the train without a ticket and the ticket conductor catches you, then you have to pay a fine of £100.
Okay, so, there's a rule in this building and that's that if you don't film in the right place,
they can just come along and stop you.
I think we're in the right place, I think we're OK.
So again, these are like facts, if this happens, this happens.
If you don't buy a ticket, you get a fine, in general.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a zero conditional.
The structure is the present simple in the if-clause, and present simple in the main or result clause.
To recap, the zero conditional is for scientific facts: If you heat water, it boils.
General truths about your personal experience: If I don't sleep well, I'm grumpy in the morning.
And rules and laws: If you don't buy a ticket, you get a fine.

title: The first conditional — likely future situations
sourceTitle: The first conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + hiện tại đơn, will + V: kế hoạch phụ thuộc thời tiết, tàu bị huỷ thì làm gì, và đưa ra dự đoán.

segments.text: Hello, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English and in this video I'll teach you how to talk about likely future situations
and their possible consequences using something called the first conditional. Let's get started.
Let's hear a very common scenario.
I asked Phil about his options for weekend plans and what they depend on.
All the plans I have depend on the weather because I need to do some work in my garden.
I can only do it if it's not raining.
So if it rains, I'll probably just stay inside and watch a film.
If it doesn't rain, I'll be out in the garden, hammering bits of wood.
So, Phil's weekend plans depend on the weather.
If it rains, he'll stay inside and watch a film.
If it doesn't rain, he'll do some work in the garden.
He's considering two likely future situations and talking about his options for both.
Now, most of us at BBC Learning English live in London, and in London,
the Underground trains and the Overground trains are often delayed or cancelled - a very real situation.
So I asked my colleagues: What will you do if your train home from the office is cancelled?
If all the Tubes are cancelled then I will cry and get three buses home.
If the train is cancelled this evening, uh, cry?
If the train is cancelled and I know before boarding the train, then I'll probably just wander around London for a bit.
Or I might get the bus, if there is a bus that I can take to my house.
Notice how George has quite a few conditions to his plans,
so if the train is cancelled and he knows before boarding the train he will wander, or walk around London for a bit.
Or he might get the bus if there is a bus to his house.
Now, because we can use the first conditional to talk about the future, it's also useful for making predictions,
like this one: If electric cars become cheaper, then more people will buy them.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a first conditional.
The structure is the present simple in the if-clause, and will plus a base verb in the main or result clause.
To recap, the first conditional is used for likely future situations and their possible consequences.

title: The second conditional — imagine & give advice
sourceTitle: The second conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + quá khứ đơn, would + V: trúng một triệu bảng, lạc trên đảo hoang, và lời khuyên "If I were you, I'd…".

segments.text: Hello, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English, and in this video we're looking at how to talk about unlikely
or hypothetical situations using something called 'the second conditional'.
Let's get into it. I asked my BBC Learning English colleagues: What would you do if you won a million pounds?
If I won a million pounds, I'd probably buy a nice little house in the countryside.
If I won a million pounds, I'd probably go travelling all round the world.
So, we have an unlikely situation - winning a million pounds.
Sadly, that doesn't happen often.
So, the second conditional is used to imagine an unlikely situation and think about the outcomes of that.
If George won a million pounds, he'd buy a house in the countryside.
Pippa would go travelling around the world.
Let's hear about another hypothetical scenario.
What would you do if you were alone on a desert island?
What would I do if I was alone on a desert island?
If I was alone on a desert island, I think I'd try to find a way to get off the desert island.
If I was alone on a desert island, I think I would be very bad at surviving.
If I were alone on a desert island, I would panic because I wouldn't know how to survive.
I would feel so lonely.
I would try to find any possible tools.
Again, an unlikely situation of being alone on a desert island.
And we're kind of dreaming and imagining: what would I do if I were in that situation?
Next, we can use the second conditional to give advice, starting with "if I were you...",
meaning 'if I were in your position' faced with the same decision or dilemma.
Listen to my colleague give me some advice about a problem.
I've run out of money this month.
If I were you, I'd ask your parents to give you a small loan so you can survive until the end of the month.
Again, this is a hypothetical situation.
"If I were you" is actually impossible - you can't become someone else.
But you're giving advice by saying, this is what I would do if I were in your position.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a second conditional.
The structure is the past simple in the 'if'-clause and 'would' plus a base verb in the main, or result, clause.
To recap, the second conditional is used to imagine an unlikely situation: If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house in the countryside.
To give advice: It's raining outside, so if I were you, I'd take an umbrella.

title: The third conditional — a different past, regrets, blame
sourceTitle: The third conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + quá khứ hoàn thành, would have + V3: tưởng tượng quá khứ khác đi, nói về tiếc nuối ("I wish I'd…") và đổ lỗi ("If you'd told me…").

segments.text: Hello, this is Georgie from BBC Learning English, and in this video,
we're looking at how to imagine a different past using something called the third conditional. Let's get started.
I interviewed my colleagues in the office.
First, I asked them how they got to work.
I got to work today by bus and then tube.
So Neil is at the office.
He arrived on the underground train - the tube.
But I asked him to think back and imagine a different scenario.
What would you have done if the tube had been cancelled?
Well, if the tube had been cancelled, I would've got a bus a bit further, and then got a train.
So again, Neil arrived at the office successfully on the tube because the tubes were not cancelled, but we're imagining a hypothetical situation where the tubes were cancelled,
and Neil has to imagine the consequences of that and what he would have done instead.
Now, Phil took the overground train to work, but I asked him what he would have done if the trains had been cancelled,
and Phil's response is very fast, but you've got the subtitles there to help you.
If the train had been cancelled, I would've got a different train which takes -
which means I'd have to get two trains and it takes about an extra fifteen, twenty minutes.
Quick note on pronunciation there.
So usually we shorten 'I would have got' to 'would've got', but Phil shortens it even more to 'I woulda got'.
So the third conditional is for imagining a different past, which means it's useful for talking about regrets.
Things we wish we could change about the past.
I asked my colleagues what they regretted.
So I had a friend in primary school and now she has children, but I'm not in touch with her.
So yeah, I wish that I'd stayed in touch with her.
If I'd stayed in touch with her, then I would've known her children.
It would've been nice to know her kids, but I don't.
Beth says she wishes she'd stayed in touch with her friend
because if she had stayed in touch with her friend, she would've known her children.
So we have a typical third conditional structure with an if-clause and a result clause.
And then we have this other common structure where we use 'wish' to express that we want something to be different.
Let's hear more examples. This is a regret that a lot of people probably have, but I wish I had studied harder at school.
I wish I'd travelled to more countries on my gap year.
Lastly, we can use the third conditional to blame someone for something they did.
Why weren't you at the meeting?
Because you didn't tell me about it.
If you'd told me about it, I would've been there.
George is saying that it's Andrew's fault that he didn't go to the meeting, because Andrew didn't tell George about the meeting.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a third conditional.
In the if-clause, we use the past perfect, and in the result clause we use 'would' plus 'have' plus a past participle.
To recap, the third conditional is for imagining a different past: If the trains had been cancelled, I would have got the bus.
To talk about your regrets: If I'd had piano lessons, I would have learnt how to read music.
And, to assign blame: If you'd told me about the meeting, I would've been there.

title: Mixed conditional — past cause, present result
sourceTitle: Mixed conditional 1 - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + quá khứ hoàn thành, would + V: việc trong quá khứ ảnh hưởng hiện tại — "If I'd slept properly, I wouldn't be so tired now."

segments.text: Hi, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English and maybe you've heard of conditionals - the zero, the first, the second, the third.
But did you know that you can mix them up to have new meanings? Let's take a look.
Now, we could say that our lives now are a result of a chain of events that happened in the past.
I live in London now because I applied for a job in the past.
Neil has another example of this.
I am so tired. I hardly slept last night.
If I'd slept properly, I wouldn't be so tired now.
So, Neil is tired now.
Why? Because he didn't sleep well in the past.
Now, this is a type of mixed conditional.
You might recognise the third conditional structure in the first part and the second conditional structure in the second part,
but we'll come back to the structure later.
For now, you just need to know that this type of mixed conditional is for expressing how your life now is affected by something that happened in the past.
Let's hear more examples. If I hadn't got this job, I would probably still be in Korea.
George used to live in South Korea.
Does he live there now?
No, he lives in London, working for the BBC.
Again, he's imagining how a past event influenced his present reality.
He got the job in the past, so now he lives in London, not Korea.
Let's hear from Pippa. So if Covid hadn't happened, I wouldn't live where I live now
because I wouldn't be able to work from home and I wouldn't be able to live outside of London.
Since the pandemic, a lot more people are able to work from home.
Now Pippa's job is in London, but because of the pandemic,
she's able to live outside of London because she doesn't have to come into the office every day.

What about Buli and Phil?
If I hadn't learnt Spanish when I was younger, my life would be very different now.
If I hadn't got married, I wouldn't be working in London right now.
OK, now you know when to use it.
But how do you use it?
Pause the video and think about which structures are used to make this type of mixed conditional.
The structure is the past perfect in the 'if' clause and 'would' plus a base verb in the main or result clause.
To recap, this mixed conditional is about how past events are affecting your life now.
If I had eaten breakfast, I wouldn't be so hungry now.

title: How to actually change your habits
sourceTitle: How to actually change your habits
description: Vì sao biết phải làm gì vẫn không đủ để thay đổi thói quen? Bí quyết nằm ở "identity" — bạn nghĩ mình là người thế nào.

segments.text: We all want to change something.
Lose weight, start a business, be more confident, get more sleep.
And there's no shortage of strategies.
5:00 a.m. routines, cold plunges, vision boards, bio hacks.
But if knowing what to do were enough, we'd all be thriving by now.
So why is it still so hard?
Studies show that people who define themselves as non-smokers are consistently more successful at quitting than those who say, "I'm trying to quit."
Why? Because when a behavior aligns with your identity, your actions naturally follow.
But when it doesn't align, when it challenges the person you've always believed yourself to be, that's when change gets hard.
If your current identity is misaligned with the change that you want to make,
whether that's a small change or a big one, the answer isn't to push harder.
It's to pause and look within.
You begin by recognizing the story that you've been living inside and then asking yourself a simple but seismic question.
What if that story isn't true anymore?

title: Can perfectionism ever be healthy?
sourceTitle: Can perfectionism ever be healthy?
description: Cầu toàn "lành mạnh" và cầu toàn "có hại" khác nhau thế nào? Học cách "dial down" và thôi tự chỉ trích bản thân.

segments.text: Is there such thing as healthy perfectionism?
In fact, there is. It's called adaptive perfectionism.
And in fact, you can be a healthy perfectionist.
You can strive at doing some things very well.
So, you can be a superb soccer player.
You can be a superb math student.
You can be a really good friend.
There are all sorts of ways to be an adaptive perfectionist that when you do something well,
you're happy, but you also know how to dial down.
That you realize that you don't have to be perfect in every aspect of your life.
Which brings us to the maladaptive perfectionist, who's somebody who can't do that.
What can you do? How can you think in a different way?
You are your own worst enemy.
Nobody is as mean to you as your own mind.
Just once write down everything you think about yourself and see how nice it is.
Because when we get up and we look in the mirror, we criticize ourselves.
We put ourselves down. I remember when I was a kid, my father used to say that I was lazy.
And I probably spent most of my adult life trying to get that voice out of my head.
Think about the voices you hear in your head.
Those are the ones that we need to re-challenge.

title: Struggling with imposter syndrome?
sourceTitle: Struggling with imposter syndrome?

segments.text: Many times, I was the only African-American in my courses, which included small group discussion,

I wasn't supposed to be good at science anyway.

those girls will perform worse than if you had not identified this negative stereotype at all.
A post-doc in my lab said to me, "Natoki, you have to get out of this habit of comparing yourself to other people.
The only person that you should compare yourself to is you.
If you can look at where you are today versus where you were 6 months or a year ago,

That's what success is. And that was a real game-changer for me.

title: How to make a good first impression
sourceTitle: How to make a good first impression
description: Vài giây đầu gặp ai đó định hình cả sự nghiệp. Cách tạo ấn tượng tự nhiên: một lời khen bất ngờ, một câu chuyện để họ kể lại.

segments.text: I study how initial perceptions, those first few seconds of meeting someone, can shift and shape career outcomes.
We can shape how others see us.
We just need to understand the perceptions at play, and the way that we all naturally, authentically delight others.
Think about someone who has made you, who has surprised you, or made you pause or reconsider them in some way.
Maybe it's someone who in a in a really serious meeting injected a brief moment of lightness.
Or someone who remembered a tiny detail that really made you feel seen.
Start with low-pressure interactions, like adding a thoughtful line to an email, or pausing and offering someone an unexpected compliment.
Finding your own natural way of disrupting the script.
Whether it's vulnerability, honesty, sensitivity, an unexpected presence that you might have.
We all have our own style of delighting others.
And finally, give them something.
Give them a story to tell.
Create a moment that they'll want to share with others.

title: How to increase your confidence — 3, 2, 1, go!
sourceTitle: How to increase your confidence
description: Muốn tự tin, hãy thay đổi hành động trước: đếm "3, 2, 1, go" rồi bước tới — câu chuyện cuộc nói chuyện khó xử trên sân bóng chày.

segments.text: Research tells us that in order to get people to change,
you need to not start with the attitudes but with the behaviors associated with those attitudes.
When people can see themselves behaving differently, they get then begin to act differently.
How would you behave or what could you achieve if you were 10 times more confident?
I've had more uncomfortable conversations than I care to recall, but one I'll share with you today,
I vividly remember standing on the warning track of the baseball field 45 minutes before game time,
looking at the opposing manager and his team wearing the wrong color uniform.
I wanted to turn and run back up to my office and hide, but instead, I faced him head-on.
And I said in my mind, 3 2 1 go, and I started walking towards him.
And when I arrived, we had a very uncomfortable conversation about his team wearing the wrong color uniform.
Yes, I had asked these grown men to change their clothes.
It was so awkward. But when I asked myself, who am I and how do I behave,
the answer was that I'm a person who's not too shy to to stand up for what I believe,
what is right, and stand up to conflict.
Counting got me started and momentum kept me going.

sourceTitle: How "creating content" killed my creativity

title: Why you might not have one true calling
sourceTitle: Why you might not have one true calling

segments.text: The notion of the narrowly focused life is highly romanticized in our culture.

The idea that we each have one great thing we are meant to do during our time on this earth
and you need to figure out what that thing is and devote your life to it.
But what if you're someone who isn't wired this way?
There is no room for someone like you in this framework.
And so you might feel alone.
You might feel like you don't have a purpose.
You might feel like there's something wrong with you.
There's nothing wrong with you.
What you are is a multipotentialite.
It is rarely a waste of time to pursue something you're drawn to even if you end up quitting.
You might apply that knowledge in a different field entirely in a way that you couldn't have anticipated.
We have a lot of complex, multi-dimensional problems in the world right now and we need creative, out-of-the-box thinkers to tackle them.

title: How to introduce yourself — and get hired
sourceTitle: How to introduce yourself—and get hired
description: Giới thiệu bản thân trong 20 từ: "soundbite, not data dump". Đừng nói về bạn, hãy nói bạn làm được gì cho người nghe.

segments.text: It doesn't matter how smart you are.

it's been said you have a better chance of engaging with a goldfish than the person that you're talking to.

Don't talk about yourself. Instead, explain what you can do for them.

I'm an award-winning best-selling author.

title: How to make decisions like a poker pro
sourceTitle: How to make decisions like a poker pro
description: Thua một ván không có nghĩa là quyết định sai. Nghĩ theo xác suất thay vì tuyệt đối — bài học từ poker cho cuộc sống.

segments.text: In Texas Hold'em, each player is dealt two cards face down.
The best possible starting hand is two aces.
When you have two aces and you're up against any other pair, the chances that aces will win is 80% of the time.
Even though you'll lose 20% of the time, you're supposed to go all-in with aces 100% of the time.
The times that you lose doesn't mean that going all-in with aces was a bad decision.
Life is also similarly probabilistic in nature as there are no guarantees and no such thing as a sure bet.
Start viewing your decisions as weighing them as the probability of something happening or the likelihood of your desired outcome against the probability of it not happening
or the likelihood of the undesired outcome and stop thinking in absolutes.
That way, you won't be afraid to make the same decision over and over again, even if it's produced a bad outcome before.
What you should focus on is the reasoning behind your decision and making sure that the basis of it is fundamentally sound.
Whether rooted in math, science, or just plain common sense.

title: Why we love Bluey
sourceTitle: Why we love Bluey
description: Vì sao phim hoạt hình Bluey được cả trẻ em lẫn bố mẹ yêu thích? Người lớn cũng mắc lỗi — và câu nói "You're doing great."

segments.text: Like most children's shows, Bluey episodes appear to be centered around some kind of life lesson.

title: Part 3: Hedging — sound less absolute
sourceTitle: 5 Methods to Develop Answers in IELTS Part 3
description: Kỹ thuật "hedging" của band 7+: tend to, may/might, many people believe, often — kèm câu trả lời mẫu về làm việc nhóm, mạng xã hội, chính phủ và ăn uống.

segments.text: Method two, hedging. Hedging is something that high-level students tend to do naturally.
Hedging means softening your language so that you don't sound too absolute or overconfident.
Instead of saying this is true, you say this tends to be true.
Instead of everyone thinks that, you say many people think that.
Why does this matter? Well, because in part three, questions are usually about complex social issues.
There are rarely simple answers.
When you hedge, you sound more academic, more thoughtful, and more fluent, and that pushes you towards band 7 and above.
The four main ways to hedge your language are: number one, using a hedging verb like tend to, seem to, appear to.
Number two, using a modal verb like may, might, or could.
Number three, using certain introductory phrases like I believe, many people think.
Number four, using certain quantifiers and adverbs like many and often rather than all and always.
So, for example, instead of saying "Elderly people enjoy going for walks in their free time," we could say "Elderly people tend to enjoy going for walks in their free time."
Or "Elderly people may enjoy going for walks in their free time."
Or "Many people believe that elderly people prefer going for walks in their free time."
Or even "Many elderly people often enjoy going for walks in their free time."
You can learn more about hedging in the PDF below this lesson.
Let's see it in action.
"Is it better to work alone or in a team?"
I'd say it really depends on the situation, but people often tend to benefit more from working in a team.
It seems that teamwork allows individuals to share ideas and solve problems more effectively,
although some people might find it difficult if there are disagreements.
Personally, I think working alone can be more productive for tasks that require deep concentration,
but in general, teams are likely to achieve better results overall.
Do you think social media has had a negative impact on society.
Well, I'd say it's had a mixed impact, to be honest.
But, while it can be useful for staying in contact with friends and family,
many people also mention how they can feel addicted to social media and waste hours away doing something that doesn't usually feel productive.
Probably the most important thing is how you tend to use social media.
Do you have control over social media, or does it have control over you?
Do you think governments should control what people eat?
Mhm. I'd say that's a rather controversial area.
On the one hand, it might be reasonable to suggest that governments have some responsibility for public health,
and that could potentially justify things like sugar taxes or restrictions on advertising unhealthy food to children.
On the other hand, many people would argue that personal freedom should be prioritized,
and that it's not really the government's place to dictate lifestyle choices.
So, I tend to think that there's a middle ground.
Light regulation, rather than outright control.

title: Part 3: The multiple perspectives method
sourceTitle: 5 Methods to Develop Answers in IELTS Part 3
description: Nhìn vấn đề từ 2–3 góc độ: from an employee's perspective, from an employer's point of view… — mẫu về làm việc từ xa, lương vs sự hài lòng, thế hệ và môi trường.

segments.text: Method three, the multiple perspectives method.
This method is fantastic for questions that ask why do people or how do different groups feel about?
The idea is simple, you consider the topic from two or three different viewpoints before giving your own conclusion.
This shows the examiner that you can think critically.
It's very much a band seven plus skill,
and it's also great if you asked to give your opinion on something you've generally not considered or thought about before.
Do you think working from home is a good idea?
I think it depends on the person and their situation.
From From an employee's perspective, working from home can be very convenient
because it saves time on commuting and allows for a better work-life balance.
However, from an employer's point of view, it might be more difficult to manage staff and ensure productivity.
Also, if we consider younger workers, they may prefer going into the office as it gives them more opportunities to socialize and learn from colleagues.
What is more important, job satisfaction or salary?
I think this really depends on the person's background and circumstances.
From one perspective, for someone who grew up in financial hardship, earning money isn't just a preference, it's a survival priority.
For them, job satisfaction might feel like a luxury they just can't afford.
However, there are also other people who feel that job satisfaction is more important.
For these people, they might be willing to accept lower pay in order to do something that fulfills them.
For me personally, I've had moments in my life where salary feels more important and other moments where satisfaction feels more important.
How do older generations and younger generations differ in their attitude towards the environment?
That's a really interesting comparison.
Generally speaking, younger generations tend to have a much stronger sense of urgency around environmental issues,
partly because they've grown up hearing about climate change, and partly because they'll live with the consequences for longer.
Older generations, on the other hand sometimes view environmental concerns through a more economic lens,
worrying that aggressive green policies could cost jobs or raise living costs.
Of course, this isn't universal.
There are plenty of older people who are deeply passionate about conservation.
But broadly speaking, there does seem to be a generate generational divide in terms of how immediate the threat feels.

title: Part 3: The rule of two
sourceTitle: 5 Methods to Develop Answers in IELTS Part 3
description: Chỉ cần hai lý do được phát triển tốt: There are two main reasons… Firstly… Secondly… — mẫu về sống ở thành phố, du lịch, làm việc tại nhà.

segments.text: Method four, the rule of two.
The rule of two is a very practical technique.
What I found is that when answering IELTS questions, it's usually pretty easy to think of two reasons or two examples,
but it gets much more difficult to give three or more reasons or examples.
So, what you can do is say things like, "There are basically two reasons why I believe that da da da."
"Firstly, da da da. Secondly, da da da."
Or "I'd say there are two ways, da da da.
Firstly, da da da. In addition, da da da.
When you do this, you're showing that you can structure your answer in a logical way, which boosts your score for fluency and coherence.
Let's see it in action.
Why do people choose to live in cities?
I think there are two main reasons why people choose to live in cities.
Firstly, cities tend to offer more job opportunities, especially in specialized fields, which makes it easier for young people to be build their career.
Secondly, urban areas have better facilities, such as public transport, health care, and entertainment options.
Because of these advantages, many people feel that city life is more convenient and provides a higher quality of life.
Why do you think tourism has increased so much in recent decades?
Well, I'd say there are two main reasons for this.
Firstly, the cost of international travel has dropped dramatically.
Budget airlines have made it possible for ordinary people to fly to destinations that would have been completely out of reach just 30 years ago.
And secondly, the rise of social media has created a kind of global inspiration engine.
People see photos of beautiful locations online and immediately want to visit them.
So, it's really a combination of accessibility and aspiration that has meant that tourism has increased so much.
What are the advantages of working from home?
Well, I can think of two significant downsides.
The first is the blurring of boundaries between work and personal life.
When your office is your living room, it becomes very difficult to mentally switch off at the end of the day, which can lead to burnout.
The second disadvantage is the loss of spontaneous collaboration.
Those informal conversations by the coffee machine or in the corridor where people where people are often get to meet and ideas are often born.
Remote work can make a team feel quite disconnected, and that can actually slow down creativity and innovation.

title: Part 3: The two most useful words — "It depends"

description: "It depends" + giải thích phụ thuộc vào điều gì: đi du lịch một mình hay cùng người khác, trẻ lớn lên ở thành phố hay nông thôn, đại học miễn phí.

segments.text: Method five, two amazing words.
Before you go to do the quizzes below this lesson, I want to tell you the two most important words in IELTS.

The two most important words are it depends.
It depends is so useful because it allows you to naturally expand on your answer.
The key is that you mustn't say it depends and stop there.
You have to follow it up by explaining what it depends on and then exploring those conditions.
That's where the marks are.
I think it depends on the person and the purpose of the trip.
If someone wants freedom and independence, traveling alone can be a better option
because they can make their own decisions and follow their own schedule.

traveling with others might be more enjoyable as it allows people to create memories together.

Personally, I'd say the ideal is somewhere in between, a smaller city or a larger town,
but I don't think there's a universal right answer here.
It genuinely depends on the family and the child.
Should university education be free for everyone?
I think it genuinely depends on the country we're talking about.
In a wealthy, high-tax nation with strong public finances, somewhere like Norway or Denmark,
free university education is absolutely viable and I think highly desirable because it removes financial barriers and creates a more equal society.
But, in lower-income countries with more pressing spending priorities, things like healthcare, infrastructure, primary education,
making university completely free might not be the most responsible use of limited public funds.
So, rather than saying yes or no outright,
I'd say the right answer depends on the economic reality of the specific country
and what its population needs most at that particular moment in time.
